entry.summary: AI agent security checklist: twenty yes/no questions on identity, permissions, data flow, injection, sandboxing, supply chain and audit, each with a link.

entry.title: An AI governance operating model for agents: who owns what
entry.summary: An AI governance operating model fails when nobody owns the agent registry, policies or budget. Roles and a RACI for platform, security, owners and reviewers.

entry.title: Ops series: how to deploy AI agents with canaries and rollbacks
entry.summary: Deploy AI agents like any service: send a new model, prompt or skill to a small share of runs first, let evals and SLOs decide and keep a rollback ready.

entry.title: Structured output for agents: schemas, contracts and ownership
entry.summary: Structured output agents hand over typed data, not free text. Define JSON schemas for tool results and outputs, version them and name an owner per contract.

entry.title: Long-running AI agents: progress files, clean states, checkpoints
entry.summary: Long-running AI agents lose context between sessions. Keep state in a feature list, progress notes and git commits to make runs resumable and auditable.

entry.title: MCP vs A2A: tools for agents versus agents talking to agents
entry.summary: MCP vs A2A: MCP connects an agent to tools and data, A2A connects agents to each other. Where each fits, what neither covers and why governance sits above both.

entry.title: Prompt injection testing: check your agents against hijacking
entry.summary: Prompt injection testing pairs a legitimate task with an injected one and checks both outcomes. Build suites for your own tools and keep containment in place.

entry.title: Code execution agents or direct tool calls? Trade-offs for builders
entry.summary: Code execution agents can cut token use sharply by filtering data in a sandbox, but need isolation. Compared with direct tool calls on cost, safety and audit.

entry.title: Ops series: LLM FinOps for agents, attributing every token
entry.summary: LLM FinOps applies the cloud playbook to agents: tag every run, attribute spend per key and team, set budgets, alert early and export usage to cost reports.

entry.title: Enterprise AI agent rollout: pilot, baseline, then scale
entry.summary: An enterprise AI agent rollout works best with a small pilot, telemetry from day one, spend limits and written exit criteria for each wider step.

entry.title: Prompt hygiene: a checklist for teams drowning in prompts
entry.summary: Prompt management for teams: a checklist covering owner, version, eval, scope and review, plus the rule to move repeated know-how into skills.

entry.title: Ops series: audit trails are not logs
entry.summary: An AI audit trail must be complete, attributable and tamper-evident; logs are for debugging. How to separate them on agent platforms and what goes where.

entry.title: NIST AI RMF for agent teams: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage in practice
entry.summary: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary and has four functions. How agent registries, data-flow maps, evals, traces and policies map to Govern, Map, Measure, Manage.

entry.title: Reading the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications as a platform team
entry.summary: How a platform team can turn the OWASP agentic top 10 and related LLM Top 10 entries into controls: least privilege, sandboxing, approvals and audit.

entry.title: Air-gapped agents: a checklist for running without the internet
entry.summary: Air-gapped AI means no downloads at run time. A checklist of what to vendor, pin and verify, and how to update agents through a reviewed import path.

entry.title: Self-hosted models for agents: what changes when inference is yours
entry.summary: Self-hosted LLM for agents: prompts stay in house, but you own capacity, updates and evaluation. Local runtimes versus batched servers and the ops work.

entry.title: BYOK for agent platforms: your keys, your providers, your bill
entry.summary: BYOK LLM explained: the platform calls model providers with your own keys and contracts. Gateways, catalogs, per-key spend tracking and BYOK's limits.

entry.title: Ops series: turning runbooks into skills without losing control
entry.summary: Runbook automation AI done safely: turn a runbook into a skill plus narrowly scoped tools with approvals. A step-by-step conversion guide for ops teams.

entry.title: AGENTS.md: one predictable place for project context
entry.summary: AGENTS.md is a Markdown file at the repository root with build steps, conventions and limits for coding agents. What belongs in it and what in skills.

entry.title: LLM as a judge: a useful grader with known biases
entry.summary: LLM as a judge scales evaluation but has position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias. Which grader to use and how to calibrate a model grader.

entry.title: LLM cost optimization for agents: caching, code execution and budgets
entry.summary: LLM cost optimization for agents: where prompt caching pays off, when code execution beats tool calls, and why hard per-run token budgets protect security too.

entry.title: Ops series: AI supply chain security and patching for agents
entry.summary: AI supply chain security for agents: inventory and patch models, MCP servers, skills, SDKs and images. A checklist for pinned, reviewed artefacts.

entry.title: Claude Code hooks as policy enforcement points for coding agents
entry.summary: Claude Code hooks run code before a tool call, so a PreToolUse hook can enforce policy locally. How to write one, where it stops and why a central gate stays.

entry.title: Claude Code vs OpenCode: a governance comparison
entry.summary: Claude Code vs OpenCode on the controls a platform team needs: permission rules, auto modes, subagents, MCP, providers and managed config. No benchmarks.

entry.title: When are multi-agent systems worth their tokens?
entry.summary: Multi-agent systems parallelise work but multiply token use and add hand-off failures. Single agent, orchestrator-worker and pipeline compared.

entry.title: Human in the loop for AI agents that works: fewer approvals, better ones
entry.summary: Human in the loop for AI agents fails when every call needs approval. Reserve people for high-risk actions, show context, and let policy handle the rest.

entry.title: AI agent sandboxing: filesystem and network isolation together
entry.summary: AI agent sandboxing works only when file access and network egress are both limited. Why one boundary is not enough and how allow-lists cut approvals.

entry.title: Ops series: AI incident response when the actor is an agent
entry.summary: AI incident response keeps the classic phases but needs a kill switch, tool revocation and policy freeze in seconds. A playbook for agent incidents.

entry.title: Workflows or agents? Choosing how much autonomy a step needs
entry.summary: Workflows vs agents is a per-step choice: fixed code paths are cheaper and easier to govern, loops are flexible. Pick the least autonomy that works.

entry.title: Versioning agent skills like any other dependency
entry.summary: Skill versioning treats agent skills as dependencies: semantic versions, changelog, pinning and evals that guard upgrades. What counts as a breaking change.

entry.title: Draw the data flow before you write the first prompt
entry.summary: An agent data flow diagram shows where untrusted data enters, where private data lives and where anything leaves. One-page template for trifecta risks.

entry.title: Ops series: SLOs for agents, from task success to time to approval
entry.summary: Define an SLO for AI agents like for any service: task success rate, consistency over trials, latency and cost per task, plus an error budget for rollouts.

entry.title: Quality gates for agent output: a checklist against slop
entry.summary: AI code quality gates let machines reject what humans should never read. A checklist of gates before review: tests, evals, size limits and policy checks.

entry.title: MCP authorization: OAuth 2.1, audiences and why passthrough is forbidden
entry.summary: MCP authorization builds on OAuth 2.1, protected resource metadata and resource indicators. How the flow works and why token passthrough is forbidden.

entry.title: Ops series: observability for agents with traces, not transcripts
entry.summary: AI agent observability works best as distributed tracing: model and tool calls become spans with tokens, cost and decisions. Use OpenTelemetry, avoid lock-in.

entry.title: Design patterns against prompt injection that do not rely on the model
entry.summary: Prompt injection design patterns like plan-then-execute, dual LLM and capability tracking limit what an attack can change by structure, not by detection.

entry.title: Tool poisoning: when the tool description is the attack
entry.summary: MCP tool poisoning hides instructions in tool descriptions that the model reads and users rarely see. How the attack works and how pinning and review limit it.

entry.title: Third-party skills are supply chain: an agent skill security checklist
entry.summary: Agent skill security starts with treating third-party skills as dependencies. A checklist for provenance, pinning, full review and least privilege.

entry.title: Ops series: change management and prompt versioning for agents
entry.summary: Prompt versioning and change management for AI agents: apply semantic versioning, review and rollback to prompts, skills and policies like code.

entry.title: Handovers are contracts: designing the seams between agents
entry.summary: An agent handover is where multi-agent systems break. Treat each one as a typed contract with an owner, a schema and an acceptance check, not a prompt.

entry.title: One MCP server per system: MCP server design you can govern
entry.summary: MCP server design rules for governable agents. One small server per system, namespaced tools, and read/write separation instead of one giant gateway.

entry.title: Small verified steps beat one big prompt: incremental agent workflows
entry.summary: Incremental agent workflows break work into small steps with acceptance checks, progress notes and a clean state after each one. Here is the pattern.

entry.title: Agent evals 101: tasks, graders and transcripts
entry.summary: AI agent evaluation checks the outcome in the environment, not just the final message. Learn tasks, trials, graders, transcripts and pass@k vs pass^k.

entry.title: Context engineering: the smallest set of tokens that does the job
entry.summary: Context engineering treats the context window as a finite budget. Practical ways to keep it small: compaction, sub-tasks with own context, notes.

entry.title: Ops series: secrets for agents never belong in the context window
entry.summary: Secrets management for AI agents in practice: keep credentials on the tool side, give the model only handles, and never pass user tokens through to downstream APIs.

entry.title: Indirect prompt injection: when the data gives the orders
entry.summary: Indirect prompt injection hides instructions in tickets, pages and tool results. Why filters fail and how to limit the blast radius by design.

entry.title: Anatomy of an agent skill: SKILL.md, progressive disclosure and scope
entry.summary: SKILL.md is the entry point of an agent skill: its short description decides when the rest loads. Progressive disclosure, a minimal skill and scoping rules.

entry.title: Ops series: identity for agents, or who is acting on whose behalf
entry.summary: AI agent identity: each agent needs its own identity plus a record of whom it acts for. Delegation vs impersonation, audience-bound tokens, no shared API keys.

entry.title: Writing tools agents can actually use: names, schemas and errors
entry.summary: Tool design for AI agents is interface design for a model reader. A checklist for names, namespaces, narrow schemas and errors, and how small tools ease policy.

entry.title: Architecture before prompts: why the foundation decides everything
entry.summary: AI agent architecture sets boundaries, contracts, handovers and data flows before any prompt runs. Why most production failures trace to a missing boundary.

entry.title: The lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content and a way out
entry.summary: The lethal trifecta in AI agents: private data, untrusted content and external communication together. How to break the triangle per agent, not trust the model.

entry.title: Too many prompts: how prompt sprawl turns into AI slop
entry.summary: AI slop is output that grows faster than anyone can review it. How prompt sprawl lowers quality, and why fewer, smaller, verified steps beat more prompts.

entry.title: What is the Model Context Protocol? A plain explanation for platform teams
entry.summary: What is MCP? The Model Context Protocol standardises how an agent host finds and calls tools, resources and prompts on servers. Plain guide for platform teams

entry.title: Running agents is operations: the old disciplines still apply
entry.summary: AI agent operations is not a new field: identity, least privilege, change management, SLOs, cost and audit all still apply. The opening of an operations series.

entry.title: Tool, skill or prompt? Three ways to give an agent what it needs
entry.summary: Agent skills vs tools vs prompts: a tool acts, a skill packages know-how loaded on demand, a prompt is standing text. Includes a decision table.

entry.title: Agent architecture is not application architecture: the agentix pattern
entry.summary: Application architecture structures code. Agent architecture decides who may do what at run time. The agentix pattern - one MCP server per system, one agent per step - is our answer.

entry.title: What is an agent harness, and why do harnesses keep shrinking?
entry.summary: An agent harness is the loop and scaffolding around a model. As models improve, much of it moves into the model or the API. What stays is governance, and that is why open-agentix treats the harness as replaceable.

entry.title: Dark software factory: only for MVPs and PoCs
entry.summary: Letting agents build software with minimal human touch can be a fast way to a prototype. open-agentix offers it as an opt-in mode with a fixed notice, and keeps approval gates for production.

entry.title: Cost is a platform concern: budgets, per-agent and per-tenant attribution, export
entry.summary: Agent systems can fail financially while working technically. open-agentix prices every step, attributes it to tenant, agent and use case, stops runs at their budget and exports the lines.

entry.title: A model may ask, the policy decides: deterministic gates and tamper-evident audit
entry.summary: In open-agentix a model can request a tool call but never authorises it. A deterministic policy gate decides before each call, and a hash-chained audit trail records what it decided.

entry.title: Least privilege for agents: decomposition instead of one all-powerful agent
entry.summary: One agent with read and write access to everything is a large blast radius. open-agentix splits a process into small agents that each hold only the tools one step needs.

entry.title: Why we are building open-agentix
entry.summary: AI agents are easy to demo and hard to operate. open-agentix is an open-source platform that takes an agent from a process description to a governed production run.
